Title: Some judge thoughts during the EC

Messages.Author: Vincent
Messages.Body:
Floppy did most of the hard work of judging, but when I wasn't
preparing something, you may have seen me helping him. As always, they
were some interesting situations:

1/ "Hey, I thought Anarch Revolt had been errated"
Yes, but many players thought they were no longer cumulative. If there
is 2 AR in play and you have no anarch, you'll lose 2 pool during your
untap. I could correct this in the last minutes of a game (because
nobody had noticed it, not even the player who was ousting his prey
with it), and I was told that on previous rounds, it had happened
also.

2/ "Wait, I think that other player also played 2 Master OOT"
The most nightmarish situation arised when I was called for the
following misplay:

Player A had attempted a rush that was DIed by his grand-prey, player
C. His Enkil Cog was also DIed by his predator, E. The funny thing is
that E, though controlling Cybele, but tapped, also played a Wash on
his predator D, and played an Ashur Tablet when I was called.
As they explained me the situation, it appeared that C (who had played
a DI on the rush, remember) had also played a Wash on B, his predator,
in that same turn.
Needless to say, many important things had happened and it couldn't be
rewind entirely, but players C and E were penalized and the other
players able to retrieve the unduly canceled cards.

3/ "Can I play another ammo?"
This one is quite frequent. A Dragon Breath's Round is DIed. The
player asks me if he can play another. The answer is yes, since no
ammo were "used".

4/ "Can I self-oust?"
I was asked twice, and in both cases it was legal. The difficulty lies
in knowing if it's dictated by collusion or not. Whether it is fair-
play or not is another thing.

Another thing, to stay related on the topic:

There is this PTW rule that causes me a lot of headache. At this years
NAC I've seen Ben Peal calling a Judge because he accused Eric Chiang
of violating the PTW rule. They were only 3 players left at the table.
I followed the table for some turns, here is my conclusion:

1. Eric did nothing forward
2. Eric seemed to give up on going forward entirely
3. But: it was clear that if Eric would go forward he wouldn't be able
to defend and be most likely ousted by Ben or at least be seriously
hurt.

So what now? Are you allowed to give up on gaining a vp and therefore
basically violating the PTW rule in order to make sure you won't get
ousted yourself? I would say yes, since you are maximizing your VP's,
since 0,5 vp is endlessly more than 0 vp.

If I am right and you are allowed to play so defensively, than what
sense does the PTW rule make? We all no that estimation of table
dynamics, players strength, etc. in v:tes is not objective, but very
much subjective. How on earth should be a judge be more competent on
this than the given player?

That's almost what happened at the EC, but it was more: A has 0, B has
2, E has 0. If E transfers out, B wins. If E doesn't transfer out, A
wins. Does E have any chance to win? No. Can E get more VPs? No. Could
E transfer out in preliminary rounds? Yes. What forbids E from
transfering out in the finals?

Indeed, transferring out would be giving some player a benefit, and
getting nothing in exchange. The benefit would be his VP.
Considering the game was going to end before time limit (which it
did), if E doesn't give his VP to a player right now, E would still
lose it to some player (might be another player) later in the game,
due to his bad position.

Ok, now let's have this example:
A has 2 VPs. A is top-seed.
D is likely to oust E, and would win his duel against A.
E doesn't have the ousting power to kill A. And even if that happened,
E definitively doesn't have the cards to oust D.
A cannot oust D.

D is in a winning position, for sure. There's enough time for him to
oust both players and get 3 VPs and the GW.

So, what happens?
A decides to self-oust.
This gives E 1 VP, 6 pool. However, E's chances of ousting D aren't
increased. D finally ousts E.
Results: A 2VP, 1st. 2nd: D (2VPs), E (1VP), B,C (0VP)

Without transferring out, A coulnd't win. That was his 0.001% win.
Was A's self-osuting legal? It definitively gave him the GW, so I
guess that was PTW.

If you're asking where I'm getting this nitpicking example, it's a
game that happened in Paris (a final, 1 year or so ago).

The question is not one of "no gain" but rather one of "loss".

When in a lost position, every action or inaction gives benefit to
someone else and no benefit to you.

> So selfoust, in my opinion, should always be considered illegal no
> matter the reason.

Playing at a loss (choosing one course of action or inaction that
results, reasonably, in achieving a lower finish that some other
action or inaction reasonably results in) is always considered
illegal, no matter the reason.

Self-ousting can be done if it is reasonably as good as all the other
available options.

On Nov 16, 10:43 am, "Kevin M." <youw...@imaspammer.org> wrote:
> "LSJ" wrote:
> > Playing at a loss (choosing one course of action or inaction that
> > results, reasonably, in achieving a lower finish that some other
> > action or inaction reasonably results in) is always considered
> > illegal, no matter the reason.
>
> If I were judging, and I was called by the other players to consider
> the "bad" play of a player, and the player when taken aside explained
> to me that his plan was to play "badly" in order to obtain VPs, I'd
> allow him to continue.  Why shouldn't I?

Playing at a loss is, by definition, not playing to obtain VPs (or, in
rare instances, playing for fewer VPs than one can reasonably get).

If, after his explanation of how he's not playing at a loss after all,
you judge that he's not playing at a loss, then of course you allow
him to continue playing not-at-a-loss.

Same as any other time a judge is called over: if the rules haven't
actually been broken, then you allow play to continue as it was.

Messages.Author: echia...@yahoo.com
Messages.Body:


Yes, occasionally transferring out can get you the win (especially if
you are of a higher seed):

A --> B --> C --> D --> E

A ousts B and C, so now it's: A --> D --> E

A and E have no vampires left (and are unlikely to influence out
more). D is simply pounding on E and will oust E soon. If A does
nothing, D will get the rest of the table (3 VP's). If A transfers
out, then E is still going to get ousted by D, but it will be a 2-2-1
split, so if A is top seed (or higher than D) than it could be good
for him to self-oust.

One potential hiccup is that if by self-ousting, A ensures that D
cannot win, there is a chance that D could self-oust (or allow himself
to be ousted) out of spite, allowing E (with no minions and almost no
pool) to win the game with 3 VP's.

This is a bit of an odd situation because even though D is in a strong
position in the game, he has actually already lost the game (though he
is still in it) because there is no reasonable way he can win. (Well,
I suppose hypothetically E could "let" D still win the game if E has
Gambit Accepted in his deck).

In contrast, if E knows he's not going to win (no minions and minimal
pool) and 1 VP is not going to be enough to win, the "everyone comes
in 2nd" rule means it doesn't matter if he's 2nd with 1 VP or 2nd with
0 VP. So if he's sufficiently pissed at A (for ruining his game, or
for being too manipulative), and would prefer that D win (instead of
A), E could play Gambit Accepted and still allow D to win the game.

In either scenario, D or E has already lost the game. (The only chance
at winning is if the other player decides to self-oust and spite
Player A, and that is certainly not a "reasonable chance" at winning.
On a similar note, if your only chance at winning is for everyone else
at the table to get disqualified or to drop dead, thereby forfeiting,
I don't consider that a "reasonable chance" either.)

>

> A player has declared that he is very likely to transfer out during
> his next influence phase.
> After having a quick look at what was happening at the table, I had to
> declare that self-ousting would be illegal with this table
> configuration at that time.

My understanding is that you should not have declared this information
to the table.

Instead, you should have remained quiet and only prevented illegal
action from occurring. Talking about self-ousting when in a non-lost
position is completely legal. Actually self-ousting is the illegal
thing that the judge should prevent.

This is relevant in the situation above (probably no consequences) and
this situation:
5 player game. Player A offers to Player B "help me oust my prey, and
then I'll self-oust." Player's C, D, and E complain that Player A
couldn't legally self-oust after that because he has reasonable
chances at more than 1 VP now. Judge is called over. Should the
judge announce to the table whether or not it would be a legal deal?
No!

If Player A attempts to actually *DO* non-PTW activities at any point
and claims it's honoring a legally made deal, then the judge can put a
stop to it if the deal wasn't legal. Talking about doing things is
totally fine, and making unenforceable deals is also fine.

If a judge can be called over at any time and announce publicly
whether or not a deal is enforceable, that removes some backstabbing
opportunities, which isn't the place of a judge. Instead, the judge
should only act when necessary - ie. when an illegal action is
actually about to happen.

Ira

I'm glad to have this discussion and this example. I posted
specifically because when I learned this, I had the same reaction as
you, Salem. Based on my understanding of what LSJ wrote on this
topic, the precise reason why the judge shouldn't answer publicly is
because of hidden information.

Also, if the policy is that judge answers when there is "enough"
public information, refusing to answer in some circumstances gives
away information.

Therefore, the correct policy is that the judge never answers publicly
and instead only stops illegal plays, or clarifies to player privately
whether or not a future action would be legal for that player only
(not some other player.)

I can know for certain from the judge if I can honor my deal, but
other players can't know.

For example:
5 player game. Player A says to Player B, "Help me oust my prey, and
then I'll self-oust." Players C, D, and E object. Player A calls
over the judge and asks if the deal will be legal. Judge answers in
private. Player A announces, "The judge just confirmed with me this
will be a legally made deal, and I will be able to keep it." Players
C, D, and E say, "Player A is a backstabbing liar and you shouldn't
believe him!" Player B has to decide who to believe.

The example above is interesting and fun for many players.

If instead the judge announced to the table that Player A's deal would
be legal or illegal, the strategic backstabbing possibilities are
reduced, and presumably fun (which should be a primary goal of game
design and these rulings, IMO.)

I hope that LSJ will correct me if I've misunderstood anything.

Ira

Brum <tiago...@gmail.com> wrote:
>I think players who are in a lost position shouldn't have the power to
>decide who wins a tournament.

By self-ousting, he grants the win to player X.

By not self-ousting, he grants the win to player Y.

He doesn't self-oust, but plays Malkavian Dementia on a copy of Zebulon
who is in torpor with zero blood. He doesn't rescue him (he can't), but
doing this grants the win to player Z.

You are, arbitrarily, blocking one of these actions but not the others -
yet the same player is deciding who wins a tournament.

All of these things, and more, can be done by players in a lost
position. They can all determine who wins the tournament. King-making
of this kind is inevitably found in pretty much every complex multi-
player game.

If players on a table find it problematic that a lost position causes
certain issues for their advancement, perhaps they should prevent a lost
position from occuring - right up until they kill the relevant
Methuselah. Rescuing that vampire cross-table may let someone hold on
until they can pull Villein. Lending someone your votes so they can
pass a Con Boon. Bouncing a bleed to your grand-predator, not your
prey. Or whatever else might be appropriate.

could've saved to get even more VPs.

will self-oust if you help me get 1 VP" and Player B agrees, I would
personally call that a deal even if Player A can't legally honor the
deal.

Consider the absurd example of Player A saying, "If you help me get 1
VP, you can take 30 pool from the blood bank." Player A can say this,
and Player B can agree to it. They can say whatever they want, and as
a judge, I will not stop them from saying that or agreeing to the
deal. Once A gets a VP and B tries to take 30 pool from the blood
bank, then I will stop them because that is the illegal play.

> keep an eye at what's happening on each of the 5 tables.

My understanding is that correct judging means that you do not
publicly reveal the validity of the deal to all players. You can
answer a question privately "Will I be able to honor this deal?" But
you don't answer, "Will this other player be able to honor the deal?"

That policy works however many tables are at the tournament - whenever
you are asked, you simply answer in private to a player asking about

By "deal" I mean an agreement two or more players reach, regarding
actions undertaken, cards played or not played, votes in favor /
against, eventually table splits / VPs assignation, etc. in which the
best interests of each player involved are reached. I will quote the
Tournaments Rule's definition of deal:

[quote]
Neither the basic game rules nor the tournament rules enforce or
regulate deals made between players. The tournament rules acknowledge
deals, however, in that a deal which represents the best interests of

the players involved at the time the deal is made is allowed to be
honored, even when the normal play to win rule would indicate that a

deal should be broken. This only applies to deal that are in the best
interests of the players involved at the time the deal is made. That
is, it applies only when making the deal is playing to win. (It is
also allowable to break such a deal, of course).
[/quote]

Deals that don't reprensent the best interests of the players involved
shouldn't be allowed (== "declared illegal"). Illegal deals can't be
made (since they're illegal). Illegal deals can be offered, but
players can't accept them. In order to know if a proposition is a
legal deal or not, a judge could be called.

If one of the terms of the deal can't be honored anymore (for
instance, a table was split 3-2, and another player ousted her prey),
I suggest players reconsider the deal.

In your example, if player A can't legally honor the deal when it
would be made, then the deal can't be made - and it ceases to be a
deal.

>

> bank, then I will stop them because that is the illegal play.

That's too absurd for me :)

declare this deal legal or illegal, I will remind that, unless a card,
rule, or judge tells a player to take 30 pool from the blood bank, she
can't take 30 pool from the blood bank. These terms are not legal
play.

> > That doesn't work with 37 tables.
>

> publicly reveal the validity of the deal to all players.  

I disagree. Some deals can end up with a player not respecting the PTW
rule (for instance: a 3-2 deal). In such cases, here's an example:
A and D agree on a 2-3 deal. The judge declares the deal legal to A
and D.
A ousts his prey, and then starts smashing down D's prey. D's prey is
a bit worried and calls a judge. Judges says (privately?) that A and D
have a deal, so that's OK for A to crush D's prey.
Had the information been public from start, D's prey would've played
differently - a counter-deal could've been done by the other players.

Deals should be made publicly, and validation / invalidation of deals
should be made publicly. Explanation on why a deal isn't legal can be
done privately, I agree.

> You can

> you don't answer, "Will this other player be able to honor the deal?"

Agreed.

> That policy works however many tables are at the tournament - whenever

> his own ability to honor a deal, or not at all to a player asking
> about someone else's ability to honor a deal.

If the deal exists, then there's no question to ask about how to honor
the deal (restrictions on "if the deal exists" were given above).
If the deal doesn't exist yet, then this question is perfectly valid
(and could end up with players making a deal). If asked privately, it
should be answered privately.

This is in the same boat as making deals. Table talk is not covered or
regulated by the rules.

The judge ruling is: the talk is not enforced by the game.

Since no other activity is happening at the time, no ruling is needed
at all.

The judge may also remind players of the rule: if the talked-about
activity (say, self-ousting) is PTW when the time comes to do it, then
it can be done.

If a deal is being made (with or without mentioning the possibility of
future self-ousting), the judge can remind players that if the deal is
PTW when it is made, it can be honored later, even if the honoring
activity is not in itself PTW.

Then, when it comes time for the player to actively or passively self-
oust or to actively or passively honor the deal in a not-in-itself-PTW
way (that is, the player has to play at a loss in order to honor the
deal), the judge can be called over to confirm that it is legal (that
is, that the self-ousting is PTW / that the deal was PTW when it was
made).

> it just seems scary. I can see how it might be fun, but I also see how it

> the time you made the deal, you could reasonably get more vps than the 1 you
> made the deal for' (say his prey was so stuffed he didn't actually need B's
> help, and his grand prey was similarly stuffed).
>

If the deal was not PTW, then it won't enable self-ousting in
violation of PTW.

If the self-ousting is still PTW when the time comes to do it (the
player is in a lost position), then it can still be done. If not, then
it is prohibited, by the rules.

Players are not allowed to waive the rules.

> I think this is what a lot of the anti self-ouster people fail to grasp.
> Not
> self ousting can help someone else just as much a self ousting. The player
> should be able to choose who to help and who to hinder.

I think everybody can grasp that just fine. What the pro self-ouster people
seem to fail to grasp is that when you are in a position where you can
self-oust (ie, no reasonable chance for a VP), you probably weren't doing a
lot in the first place. Because if you were, you wouldn't be allowed to
self-oust. Given that, continuing that inaction will not unbalance the table
due to your doing, but instead the game will just continue as it were for
another turn. And another if need be. Therefore, a lot of people believe
that self-ousting is *more* kingmaking than not self-ousting is. If you are
in a position where you are currently allowed to self-oust, you shouldn't
get some arbitrary power to give your predator a VP and six pool and in the
process have a big say in who will win the table. You were ousted. Don't try
and influence the table with your idiotic moves and just play the game. Deal
for half a VP for all I care.

Also, self-ousting is only really an issue in the case where your
grandpredator is right about to oust your prey. If I'm doing everything I
can to oust my prey before he can oust his prey, even cooperating with my
grandprey to keep him alive longer (for example voting in favor for extra
voter cap love) and in the turn I'm about to get my prey my grandprey
decides he will self-oust for a a VP I will feel robbed and I will be
pissed. I've had people pull this on me with giving complete crap as
"because your sleeves are ugly" or "because you play auspex" as reason why
my prey should get the VP instead of me getting the double VP. This kind of
crap makes a given the game un-fun and discourages clever, strategic play
and deckbuilding over "WAAAAAAAAA NEED TO NUKE PREY RAWRR!!!!"-play. Well,
that and DI.

I believe self-ousting by transfers should stop. I don't care about other
means because in the real world all these fuzzy and fluffy self-oust actions
that everyone always comes up with don't actually happen. Clearly as long as
LSJ is in charge of the rules (which is, I may add, a GOOD thing) this won't
happen. And with it a ton of annoying judging discussions come up. I can
think up dozens of examples where after the first crypt cards enter the
controlled region I knew I would get zero VP. Blindly looking at the rules,
given I have absolutely no chance at getting a VP, I can do whatever I like,
including making 8 turns of transfers and go grab a beer at the bar. It's
pretty obvious a judge won't allow me to, but where do we draw the line?
"Reasonable" is a vague term to begin with and especially in a multiplayer
game where reaching the time-limit actually awards you with 0,5 VP you
should always try to get at least a VP. On Day 2 of the EC a few weeks ago,
I snatched up a VP from a completely lost position just by not self-ousting.
In this case my predator wasn't sure he'd win the heads-up with my prey
while was completely sure he would win the heads-up with me. You never know
what happens. Just because you can't get a VP on your own, doesn't mean
you'll end up getting nothing by just trying to hang on.

If you're not self-ousting you are playing the game. If you are self-ousting
you are kingmaking.

The player is using future tense in this question. I was assuming the
question was asked before the deal was made. Thus, the player is
asking if the deal she's going to make will respect the PTW rule.
That's an information I think should be given, and should be given
privately in this case (since the player asked privately).

If the player asks, once the deal is made, "Can I honor the deal
[rather than the PTW rule]?" (adding the [...], because I'm sure we're
not discussing about a player who couldn't see what cards in his hand
she should play to respect the deal), the big difference is that the
deal is made. This means either it was PTW when made, and then the
answer lies in the past (and is yes, and should be public, imho), or
the deal was not PTW when made (and the answer is obviously "no",
publicly), or something happened that caused the deal to not be doable
anymore, in which case I'd say "reconsider the deal".

Player A gets to know (in private) if Player A could honor the deal if
it were made now.
Player A should know if Player A can honor a deal that was made
previously (by asking the judge if, at that time, the deal was PTW).
Player B should know if Player A can honor the deal if it were made
previously (by asking the judge if, at that time, the deal was PTW).
"Player A can honor a deal that was made previously" is a public
information.
Player B can ask (privately) if Player A could honor the deal if it
were made now. I'm not sure I'd answer this question in any other
manner than by estimating the public information of the table and
giving B a private answer. Involving any hidden information (A's hand,
B's hand, ...) could lead to different answers to different players,
which is bad.

1) The same way the question was asked, especially if A doesn't
involve non-public information in his question. This is: If A asks
privately, the answer should be given privately. If A asks publicly
and doesn't add "given the fact that I have ... in my hand", the
answer could be given publicly with the public information. If A asks
publicly, but gives the judge a hidden information, the answer should
not be public, since it involves non-public information (whether that
information matter or not isn't relevant).
2) If that information could be given from public information, then
the judge should give it the same way it was asked. If that
information requires some knowledge of hidden information that B
doesn't have, then the judge shouldn't answer. B's hidden information
shouldn't be relevant here, since A doesn't know of it.

If you meant 'position where it was reasonable that I wouldn't get another

actions and card draws allowed you to grab another VP, then sure. Go you.
But by definition, that was unlikely to happen, so you should have been able

could conceivably have been expected, then you weren't really in a position
where it was unreasonable to get more VPs, and thus you shouldn't have been
allowed to self-oust if you'd wanted to.

Don't get me wrong, I myself struggle on to the very last 99.99% of the
time, even when I don't expect it to help. That's how I play. But I don't
hold it against people who want to bail if they're fucked.

without actually being pretty fucked. But I can't rule against people being
bad players and not being able to see their opportunities. No one can.
